variants.name: Template-template policies with policy inheritance (classic)
variants.idiom_name: template<template<class> class Policy> host inheriting its policies
variants.implementation_notes: The form documented in Modern C++ Design: each policy arrives as a template-template parameter and the host inherits from it (publicly for enrichment, privately for implementation reuse), so a policy can add members that the host never names and optional functionality degrades gracefully when a policy lacks them. Still the right choice when a policy must be instantiated for a type only the host knows, and when policies are expected to enrich the host's interface; the cost is denser code, weaker diagnostics before concepts, and policy members becoming part of the host type.
pitfalls: Public inheritance from policies leaks their members into the host's interface (that is the point) and makes `delete policy_ptr` well-formed unless the policy declares a protected non-virtual destructor.
Template-template parameters cannot carry policies that need extra type arguments (an allocator's value type, a comparator's key type); switch to the type-parameter form or an alias template.

variants.name: Type-parameter policies with defaults (modern C++)
variants.idiom_name: template host with defaulted type-parameter policies (C++11)
variants.implementation_notes: Modern C++ default: the host is a class template whose policy parameters are ordinary types with defaults (template<class T, class Ownership = RefCounted<T>, class Threading = SingleThreaded>), the policies are duck-typed so the host simply calls their members, and `using` declarations or private inheritance pull policy members in only when the host wants to expose them. Contracts are enforced at the instantiation site with C++20 concepts (or static_assert on older standards). The classic template-template form remains justified when a policy must be instantiated for a type the host only knows internally, and public inheritance from policies when a policy should add members the host never names.
pitfalls: A policy member the host never calls is never checked: with the duck-typed contract a misspelled member in an unexercised policy compiles silently until an enriched host function first uses it.
Private inheritance from several policies needs the empty base optimization to stay free; verify with static_assert(sizeof(Host) == sizeof(state)) after adding stateless policies.
Policies whose axes interact (ownership with conversion, checking with storage) compile into semantically wrong combinations; express the compatibility requirement as a static_assert or a concept.

variants.name: Concept-constrained policies (C++20)
variants.idiom_name: requires-clauses and named concepts on the policy parameters
variants.implementation_notes: C++20 moves the implicit policy contract into a named concept (template<class P> concept EvictionPolicy = requires(P p, std::string_view k) { { p.evict(k) } -> std::same_as<void>; };) and constrains the host's parameters with it, so a non-conforming policy fails at the instantiation site naming the unsatisfied requirement instead of producing a cascade from inside the host body; the realization is otherwise identical to the C++11 type-parameter form, so use it whenever the toolchain is C++20. Concepts are still syntactic: they prove the members exist, not that the policy behaves as documented.
pitfalls: Concepts check expressions, not semantics: a policy that models the concept but violates the documented meaning still compiles and runs wrong.
Over-constraining rules out valid policies (a non-copyable lock policy, a policy whose members are private); constrain exactly the members the host actually uses.
